Taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill

When everything on offer is good enough, how do you know which one is right?

Section 1A Tuesday in Bengaluru with thirty-four good answers

On Tuesday, 3 February 2026, at about seven in the evening, Meera Rajagopalan had thirty-four versions of the same screen open across two monitors in Vibhava Money's office off Bannerghatta Road. Vibhava Money is a consumer investing app: eleven lakh monthly active users, mostly first-time mutual-fund investors in tier-one and tier-two Indian cities, competing for attention against far larger names. The screen in question was the one users would see immediately after their first SIP — a systematic investment plan — was set up. It had to do three things: confirm the money was committed, explain what would happen on the tenth of every month, and make a nervous twenty-six-year-old feel that she had done something sensible rather than something irreversible.

Six weeks earlier, producing three candidate designs for that screen would have consumed a designer for a fortnight. On this Tuesday, Meera's team had generated thirty-four in a day and a half — full layouts, real copy, real illustration, each one built from the same design system and each one plausible. Her design lead in Berlin, Anjali Sridhar, had reviewed all thirty-four and written back a single line at 3 a.m. Central European Time: None of these are bad. That is the problem.

The deadline was not negotiable. Vibhava's tax-season traffic — the annual scramble in February and March, when salaried Indians buy equity-linked savings schemes before the financial year closes on 31 March — was already building. Product marketing had booked the release train for 14 February. Roughly 40,000 new investors would see whichever screen Meera picked, in the six weeks that matter most in the Indian retail-investing calendar. Get it right and Vibhava's first-SIP-to-second-SIP continuation rate, currently 71 per cent, might move two or three points. Get it wrong and the cost was not a crash or an outage; it was something quieter and worse — a screen that was perfectly competent and left no impression at all.

Meera's problem was not a shortage of options. It was that she had no defensible way to reject thirty-three of them. That gap — between abundance and selection — is what this page is about.

Section 2The idea: a standard you can state before you look

Figure 1. The structural change behind the topic. Nothing here says the generated options are excellent; it says they are adequate, and that there are many of them. Scarcity moves to whoever can reject well.

Start with definitions, because both words in "editorial judgement" are used loosely. Taste, in the sense used here, is not a private preference and not an aesthetic sensibility. It is a standard for selection that its holder can state, apply consistently, and defend to someone who disagrees. Editorial judgement is the act of applying that standard to a set of candidate artefacts — copy, designs, flows, model outputs, roadmap items — in order to keep one and reject the rest. The editor's characteristic move is not creation; it is a reasoned refusal.

The problem the idea was invented to solve is old and not originally a technology problem. Magazine and book editors have worked this way since at least the nineteenth century: the manuscript pile is large, most of it is publishable, and the editor's value is knowing what the publication is for. Film editing formalised it further — Walter Murch's much-cited "rule of six", published in the 1990s, ranks the criteria for choosing a cut in strict order, with emotion first and spatial continuity last, precisely so that an editor facing several acceptable cuts has a principle rather than a mood. Industrial design produced its own written standards, most famously Dieter Rams's ten principles for good design in the 1970s, which exist to make "I like this one" into an argument. Product management borrowed the vocabulary late, calling it "product sense" in the 2010s and largely leaving it undefined.

What changed between roughly 2023 and 2026 is arithmetic, not philosophy. When a generative model can produce a competent screen, a competent PRD section, a competent SQL query or forty competent variants of onboarding copy in minutes, the binding constraint on quality stops being production capacity. Figure 1 shows the shape of it. The scarce input becomes the standard against which the abundance is filtered — and unlike production, that standard cannot be generated by the same model, because the model has no stake in what your product is for.

The sentence Meera could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "Taste is not knowing which one I like. It is having written down, before I looked, what this screen has to do — and then rejecting everything that does not do it, out loud, with reasons."

Section 3How it actually works, step by step

Practitioners who do this well follow a recognisable sequence. Most of them do not describe it, which is why it looks like intuition from the outside. Written out, with Meera's screen as the running example, it has eight steps, and three of them are almost always left implicit.

One: name the moment, not the artefact. Meera's brief was initially "design the post-SIP confirmation screen". That is an artefact. The moment is: a twenty-six-year-old in Coimbatore has just committed ₹2,000 a month of her salary for the first time, on a phone, at 11 p.m., possibly without telling anyone. Everything downstream depends on which of those two framings you write at the top of the page.

Two: write the standard before generating. This is the step that separates the discipline from post-hoc rationalisation. Meera's team wrote four criteria on the Monday, before a single variant existed: the screen must (a) make the recurring commitment unmistakable, (b) be comprehensible to someone who does not know the words "NAV" or "folio", (c) offer a visible, unfrightening way to change or stop the SIP, and (d) feel like a beginning rather than a transaction receipt. Criteria written after you have seen the options are not criteria; they are descriptions of your favourite.

Three: rank or weight the criteria, and name at least one disqualifier. A disqualifier is a condition whose violation removes a candidate regardless of its other merits. Vibhava's was regulatory and non-negotiable: the mandatory market-risk disclosure required in Indian mutual-fund communication had to be legible on the first viewport, not behind a scroll or a tooltip. Ordering matters more than most teams admit. Murch's insight was that a ranked list resolves ties that a weighted average obscures.

Four: generate deliberately, not maximally. Abundance is useful only if it is varied. Thirty-four variants that differ in corner radius are one variant. Meera's instruction to the team was to produce variants along three explicit axes — tone (warm, neutral, institutional), information density (one idea per screen versus three), and what the screen leads with (the money, the date, or the goal).

Five: eliminate before you compare. The first pass is not ranking; it is applying the disqualifier. Eleven of the thirty-four pushed the risk disclosure below the fold. They were gone in nine minutes. This step is cheap and enormous, and skipping it is why review meetings run long.

Six: write the kill note. For each rejected survivor, a single sentence stating which criterion it failed and how. This is the most-skipped and most-valuable step. It converts taste into something transmissible: a junior PM who reads twenty kill notes learns the standard faster than from any amount of praise for the winner.

Seven: check the standard against known exemplars. Before trusting the criteria, run them over one screen everyone already agrees is good and one everyone agrees is poor. If the standard ranks the bad one highly, the standard is broken, not the candidate.

Eight: decide who decides, and record it. Editorial judgement is singular by design. Committees average, and averages have no taste. Meera's team had a written rule: the group PM chooses, the design lead holds a veto on the disqualifier only, and the choice plus its reasoning goes in the release note.

Figure 2. The editorial loop at Vibhava Money. The arrow that matters runs leftward: rejections feed back into the written standard, which is how a private judgement becomes an organisational capability.

Notice what the leftward arrow in Figure 2 does. Without it, each selection is a one-off act of intuition and the organisation learns nothing; the next PM starts from zero and the senior person becomes a bottleneck. With it, the standard accumulates. This is the honest answer to the contested question of whether taste can be taught: the underlying sensibility may or may not be teachable, but the standard — the written, argued, exemplified version of it — demonstrably is.

Section 4A worked example, with the arithmetic shown

Six candidates survived Vibhava's disqualifier and the first criteria pass. Meera's team scored each on the four criteria, 1 to 5, and applied the weights they had agreed on the Monday: commitment clarity 0.30, comprehension 0.30, reversibility 0.20, and "feels like a beginning" 0.20. The weighted score for variant V-07 is therefore (4 × 0.30) + (5 × 0.30) + (3 × 0.20) + (3 × 0.20) = 1.20 + 1.50 + 0.60 + 0.60 = 3.90. Table 1 shows the full set.

Suppose the customer-success lead in Singapore, Farida Qureshi, is right that Vibhava's real leak is not enthusiasm but confusion — that users who cancel in month two mostly say they did not realise the debit repeated. Two lessons follow, and the second is the important one. First, the ranking is not robust: a defensible change to a single weight reverses it. Second — and this is what a numerate PM must internalise — the arithmetic did not make the decision. The disagreement between Meera and Farida is about what the product is for at that moment, and it was always going to be. The scoring table is valuable because it located the disagreement precisely, in one weight, rather than letting it play out as a two-hour argument about which screen felt nicer. That is the correct use of quantification in a taste decision: not to replace judgement, but to make the judgement small, visible and arguable.

Section 5Nuances a learner must become aware of

Taste is a standard, preference is a reflex

People blur these constantly. "I don't like the orange" is a preference; "the orange competes with the primary call to action, and our standard says one focal point per screen" is a standard. The test is whether a colleague who disagrees can tell what evidence would change your mind. If nothing would, you have a preference, and preferences do not survive contact with a competent peer.

Selection requires variance, and generated abundance often has none

Models trained on the same corpus, prompted from the same brief, produce options that cluster. Thirty-four variants can easily be four ideas wearing thirty-four coats of paint. Before congratulating yourself on a wide funnel, ask what the axes of genuine difference are and count distinct answers on each. Vibhava's thirty-four collapsed to eleven meaningfully distinct approaches, and knowing that changed how much confidence the exercise deserved.

Polish is not quality, and generated work is uniformly polished

The historical signal for effort — clean typography, complete copy, no placeholder text — used to correlate with care and therefore with quality. Generation severs that link. Every option now arrives looking finished. Reviewers who learned to read polish as a proxy are, without noticing, reading noise. The discipline is to evaluate the argument the artefact makes, not its finish.

The standard must be written before the options are seen

This is the single highest-leverage rule and the hardest to keep. Human judgement is fluent at constructing criteria that happen to be satisfied by whatever it already prefers. Writing the standard first does not remove bias; it makes it auditable, because the criteria and the choice are separately visible and can be checked against each other.

Editorial judgement does not tell you whether the set was worth choosing from

This is the sharpest limit of the idea. A perfectly executed selection over thirty-four mediocre options yields the best mediocre option. Nothing in the method detects that the whole set is beneath the bar, and the ritual of scoring can create false comfort. The countermeasure is to keep at least one external reference in the comparison — a screen from a product you admire, not necessarily a competitor — and be willing to conclude that none of your candidates clears it.

It is routinely confused with veto power and with "vision"

A senior person who rejects work without articulating a standard is exercising authority, not taste, and the tell is that their team cannot predict their decisions. Vision, meanwhile, concerns what to build over years; editorial judgement concerns which of these things to ship this week. They can point in opposite directions, and an honest practitioner says which one they are using.

Consistency over time matters more than correctness on any one call

A team can absorb a wrong choice. What it cannot absorb is an unpredictable chooser, because unpredictability makes preparation impossible and pushes everyone to hedge. The measurable proxy is simple: can a mid-level PM on your team predict which variant you will pick, before you pick it, at better than chance? At Vibhava that number was tracked informally and was about six in ten — improving, but not yet a shared standard.

The questions a thoughtful newcomer should ask

Before relying on this method, ask three things. What is the disqualifier here, and who has the authority to set it? What would make me reject every option in front of me? And, most uncomfortably, what would I have to observe after launch to conclude that my standard — not my choice — was wrong? A standard with no falsifying observation attached is a taste claim dressed as a process.

Section 6How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the standard is usually about feeling and comprehension, and the feedback loop is fast: Vibhava can learn within three weeks whether the chosen screen moved second-SIP continuation. Because feedback is fast, the temptation is to skip the standard and let experimentation decide. That works when the option space is small and the metric is honest, and fails when the differences between options are too fine to reach significance at your traffic — which, at eleven lakh monthly users with a 40,000-user cohort, is most copy-level differences.

In B2B software the standard is usually about fit with a workflow the buyer already has, and the feedback loop is months long. Editorial judgement carries more weight there precisely because you cannot test your way out: an enterprise buyer will not see thirty-four variants. A B2B PM's standard tends to include criteria a consumer PM never writes down — what the customer's compliance officer will say, whether an implementation consultant can explain it in a training session, whether it survives translation into a procurement document.

In marketplaces the standard has to hold for two populations with opposed interests, so a single scoring table is usually wrong. The disciplined version scores each option twice — once as a seller, once as a buyer — and treats a large gap between the two scores as information rather than as an average to be taken.

Stage changes the practice more than product type does. In a twenty-person company the founder's taste is the standard, it lives in their head, and that is efficient: the cost of writing it down exceeds the cost of asking them. Somewhere past about eighty people the arithmetic reverses, because the founder becomes a queue. Large organisations then face the opposite failure: standards written so abstractly ("delightful", "trustworthy") that they disqualify nothing. A standard that cannot reject a real candidate is decoration.

Section 7Common mistakes

Scoring theatre. The symptom, visible from outside, is a beautifully weighted matrix whose top-ranked option happens to be the one the senior person mentioned favourably in the kickoff. The underlying misunderstanding is that quantification produces objectivity. The cheapest diagnostic: check whether the weights were recorded before the scores; if they share a timestamp, the matrix is a justification, not a decision.

Averaging by committee. The symptom is a shipped artefact that nobody in the room would have chosen individually. The misunderstanding is that combining tastes improves them; in fact averaging strips the distinctive element from each option, which is usually the only thing that made it worth choosing. Diagnostic: ask each reviewer to name their first choice privately before discussion. If the group's outcome matches no individual's first choice, you have averaged.

Mistaking abundance for exploration. The symptom is a team that generates more options every cycle and takes longer to decide each time. The misunderstanding is that more candidates raise the ceiling; past a point they only raise the cost of comparison and the chance of arbitrary choice. Diagnostic: count distinct approaches, not distinct files. If the ratio is worse than about one in three, stop generating and start rejecting.

Refusing to state the standard because it feels reductive. The symptom is a leader who says "you'll know it when you see it" and whose team ships increasingly cautious work. The misunderstanding is that articulating a standard destroys the sensibility behind it. Diagnostic: ask the leader to write kill notes for three rejected options. If they cannot, the sensibility may be real but it is not yet transferable, and the organisation is one resignation away from losing it.

Section 8What good looks like

Handled well, the same decision is unremarkable to watch. The standard exists in writing before the work starts and fits on half a page. Generation is deliberately varied along named axes. The disqualifier removes a third of the field in the first ten minutes and nobody argues, because it was agreed in advance. The remaining comparison is short, because the criteria are ranked and most candidates fail an early one. Every rejection has a one-line reason attached, and those lines are readable a quarter later by someone who was not in the room. The person who decides is named, decides alone, and writes down why — including which criterion they knowingly sacrificed, because a choice that sacrifices nothing has not been made. And after launch, the team returns to the standard, not only to the metric, and asks whether the criteria predicted what actually happened.

Section 9What Meera decided

On 5 February, Meera chose V-19, the date-led variant — the one that wins only under Farida's weights. Her reasoning, recorded in four sentences in the release note, was that Vibhava's evidence about month-two cancellations was real and specific, while the case for "feels like a beginning" rested on a general belief about first-time investors that nobody had tested. Where evidence and instinct point in different directions on a criterion's weight, she wrote, the weight follows the evidence, and the instinct becomes next quarter's experiment. She also recorded what she was giving up: V-19 is the least warm of the six, and if continuation improves while app-store sentiment falls, that trade will be visible and she will have been wrong in a way she can name.

What to learn next follows directly. Reviewing work you did not write is the mechanics of the same skill applied to text and code rather than screens, and it is where most PMs will exercise editorial judgement daily. Reasoning about trade-offs supplies the vocabulary for the sacrifice Meera recorded. And What a junior PM should learn first now asks the question this page has deliberately left contested: if selection has become the scarce skill, and selection depends on a standard, where does a twenty-four-year-old with no standard yet begin?

Two questions to sit with.

1. Think of the last artefact you approved at work. Could you write, in one sentence each, the reasons you rejected the alternatives — and would a colleague who read only those sentences be able to predict your next decision?

2. If your standard cannot reject any of the options currently in front of you, is that evidence that the options are all excellent, or that your standard is decorative? How would you tell the difference before shipping?

Aarambh Storefronts: twelve good shops and one Navratri

Jaipur, August 2026. Nine thousand merchants, twelve adequate storefronts each, and one decision about who chooses.

Section 1The opening

On Thursday, 20 August 2026, at half past nine in the morning, Nandita Bhargava sat in Aarambh Storefronts' office on Tonk Road in Jaipur with a printout she had made against her own habit. It showed twelve versions of the same online shop: Meena Handicrafts, a lac-bangle seller in Sanganer with forty-one products and an Instagram following of 3,200. Twelve complete storefronts, each generated in under two minutes — logotype, colour palette, category structure, product descriptions written from photographs, a festive banner. Nandita had spent forty minutes with the printout. She could rank them. She could not, at first, say why.

Her deadline was 5 September. Aarambh's festive onboarding cohort — 9,000 new merchants signed up for the Navratri and Diwali season, the largest single intake in the company's history — would begin going live on 21 September. Whatever the product did with those twelve options, it would do nine thousand times before Dussehra, and the storefronts would stay up for years. The engineering work was finished. The only thing unresolved was who chose, and against what standard.

Section 2Company background

Aarambh Storefronts was founded in 2021 by two former payments engineers who had watched small merchants in Rajasthan and western Uttar Pradesh get onto UPI in a matter of months and then stall completely at the next step. Accepting a payment was solved; having a shop worth sending a customer to was not. Aarambh's product built a merchant a web storefront, published it to the ONDC network so that buyers on participating apps could discover it, handled catalogue and inventory, and settled payments through a Razorpay integration with GST-compliant invoicing.

By August 2026 the company served 68,000 active merchants at ₹399 a month for the standard plan, giving annual recurring revenue of about ₹27 crore, plus a small take rate on ONDC-originated orders. Its merchants were apparel and handicraft sellers in Jaipur, Surat, Tiruppur and Ludhiana; food and spice brands in Kerala and Andhra; and a growing tail of home-services businesses. They were not the merchants who could afford an agency, and they were not the merchants who would ever open Shopify's theme editor. Many of them also sold on Meesho and Flipkart and took orders on WhatsApp; Aarambh's pitch was that the storefront was the shop they owned, as opposed to the shelf they rented.

The generated-storefront feature, internally called Roop, had been in build since February. Until Roop, a merchant chose one of six fixed templates and typed their own product descriptions, which most of them did badly or not at all: 46 per cent of Aarambh storefronts had at least ten products with no description longer than four words. Roop removed that barrier entirely. It also created the problem Nandita was holding.

Section 3The situation

In July, Aarambh ran a pilot on 1,200 merchants across three cities. Half were shown all twelve generated storefronts and asked to pick one. Half were shown a single storefront chosen by Aarambh's four-person content and design team in Jaipur, working to a written standard, with a "show me another" button. The results, in Exhibit 1, were not what anyone had predicted, and they were read differently in four time zones.

Lea Hoffmann, Aarambh's design lead, works from Berlin and joined from a European commerce platform in 2024. She had built the written standard used by the Jaipur team: five criteria, of which the first was that a first-time visitor must be able to tell what the shop sells within two seconds, and the disqualifier was that the shop's own name must never be rendered in a decorative face at a size smaller than the banner headline. She had watched the pilot recordings and was blunt in the Monday review at 6 a.m. her time: merchants shown twelve options chose, with striking consistency, the busiest one.

Sanjana Rao, customer-success lead in Singapore, had a different set of evidence. Her team ran the merchant support line, and merchants who had been given a choice were, by her count, markedly happier — they described the store as theirs, they filled in more catalogue fields afterwards, and they churned less in the first thirty days. She was not disputing Lea's aesthetic reading. She was disputing that it mattered more than ownership.

Aditya Ramanathan, the data scientist in Toronto, had the thirty-day sales figures and refused to interpret them for anybody. The merchant-chosen cohort had higher catalogue completion and higher retention. The editor-chosen cohort had higher visitor-to-order conversion on ONDC-originated traffic. Both effects were real and they pushed in opposite directions on gross merchandise value.

Section 4The people

Nandita Bhargava, Head of Product, Jaipur, joined from a payments company in 2023 and owns the Roop decision. What she wants is a rule she can still defend in March, when the storefronts are six months old and someone asks why they all look the same, or why they all look different.

Lea Hoffmann, design lead, Berlin. She wants Aarambh to hold a standard and ship one storefront, arguing that the merchant's judgement about their own shop is not the same as judgement about a stranger's two-second impression of it. Her private worry is that 68,000 storefronts with no editorial floor become a network that buyers on ONDC learn to distrust.

Sanjana Rao, customer-success lead, Singapore. She wants merchant choice. Her argument is commercial rather than sentimental: a merchant who feels the shop is hers finishes her catalogue, and a finished catalogue is worth more than a tasteful banner. Her team also carries the support load, and Exhibit 1 shows choice costs her 15 extra contacts per 100 merchants.

Ishaan Kulkarni, engineering lead, Pune. He wants to build an automatic evaluator: score all twelve against the editorial team's rankings, ship the top one plus two alternates. He can have it working by 2 September. He has not said, though he believes it, that a four-person editorial team in Jaipur cannot survive contact with 9,000 merchants in three weeks.

Vikram Sethi, sales head, New Jersey, has a signed letter of intent from Al Shurooq Retail, a Dubai group that wants to bring 400 Indian handicraft sellers onto a diaspora storefront by Diwali, at ₹1.2 crore for the first year. Al Shurooq's buying team has said plainly that the storefronts must look consistent, because they will sit inside Al Shurooq's own branded marketplace. Vikram does not much mind how Nandita gets there.

Option B, the one Lea wants, needs 1,350 editorial hours against 480 available, so it exists only if Aarambh hires seven contract editors in a fortnight and trains them on a standard that currently lives in four people's heads. Option C's cost is small, but the number in the last row is a promise, not a measurement, and the support estimate is Sanjana's guess about a system nobody has run.

Section 6The options

Option A: give the merchant all twelve. Upside: it ships without new cost, onboarding completion is 7 points higher, merchants finish their catalogues, and Sanjana's retention argument is supported by the only thirty-day data Aarambh has. Cost: median GMV is ₹3,500 lower per merchant, ONDC conversion is nearly a full point worse, support contacts nearly double, and Aarambh has no answer for Al Shurooq's consistency requirement.

Option B: the editorial team picks one, with a regenerate button. Upside: the strongest sales outcome in the pilot, the lowest support load, an answer for Dubai, and a written standard that improves with use. Cost: ₹21.6 lakh and seven contract editors hired and calibrated in three weeks, and a real risk that seven new editors applying a five-line standard produce inconsistency worse than the machine's.

Option C: build an evaluator on the editors' rankings and ship the top one plus two alternates. Upside: it scales, it costs ₹6.4 lakh, and it offers a middle path between imposed and chosen. Cost: the evaluator is trained on roughly 7,200 scored storefronts from one team in one city, its behaviour outside that distribution is unknown, and there is no time to audit it before 21 September.

Section 7Questions for discussion

1. What exactly is the standard Aarambh is selecting against? Write it in one sentence, and say whose interest it serves — the merchant's, the buyer's, or Aarambh's.

2. Exhibit 1 shows merchant choice winning on engagement and losing on sales. Which of those two is the better proxy for the outcome Aarambh should care about over two years, and what evidence would settle it?

3. Exhibit 2 is presented as evidence that merchants choose badly. State the strongest case that merchants are choosing correctly and the editors are wrong.

4. It is 20 August. What does Nandita ship on 21 September, and what does she tell Vikram to promise Al Shurooq?

Section 8A note for the learner

The lens for this case is editorial judgement under abundance: when generation is cheap and every option is adequate, the scarce input is a stated standard and the discipline to reject against it. Notice what Aarambh actually lacks. It does not lack storefronts, engineering capacity or data. It lacks an agreed answer to one question — what is an Aarambh storefront for? — and every disagreement in the case is that question wearing a different costume. Lea's standard optimises a stranger's two-second impression. Sanjana's optimises the merchant's sense of ownership. Vikram's optimises a Dubai buyer's need for consistency. All three are legitimate; they are simply not the same standard, and no volume of variants will reconcile them.

A well-reasoned answer therefore begins by naming the standard rather than by choosing an option. It should also treat Exhibit 2 carefully: a chart showing merchants departing from an editorial ranking is evidence of divergence, not of error, and a learner who reads it as proof that merchants have poor taste has skipped the step that matters. Taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill

Selection under abundance: why the precision of your standard now matters more than the width of your funnel.

Section 1Two decisions, one week apart

In Pune, on Monday 9 March 2026, Devika Menon, VP Product at Kausalya Systems, was holding a decision she had already deferred twice. Kausalya sells field-service software to companies that maintain lifts, chillers and diesel gensets across India — 240 enterprise customers, about ₹190 crore of annual recurring revenue, technicians in roughly 900 Indian towns. The new feature was mundane on its face: after a technician closes a job, the system drafts the service report automatically from the job log, photographs and parts list. The drafting worked. The problem was that Devika's team had produced nine distinct report voices — nine ways of writing the same facts — and every one of them read acceptably. A terse one. A narrative one. One that led with the fault code. One built as a table with a two-line summary. Her staff engineer in Bengaluru, Suraj Kamath, had put it precisely in the review: "There is no version of this we would be embarrassed to ship. There is exactly one version we should ship, and I cannot tell you which."

In Mumbai, four days later, Rohit Deshmukh at Malhaar Audio faced the same structural problem at a different order of magnitude. Malhaar is a consumer audio app — music, podcasts and long-form Marathi and Hindi spoken word — with 62 lakh monthly actives and a business that depends on people opening the app without a specific intention. From April the app would generate personalised daily mixes with machine-written titles, blurbs and cover art: roughly 4,000 new artefacts a day at launch, rising to 40,000 within a year. Nobody was going to review 40,000 of anything. Rohit's editorial team of five, led by Sneha Iyer, could look at perhaps sixty a day with care. The question was not which blurb to ship. It was what a standard even means when the thing being judged is a distribution rather than an artefact.

These two decisions form the spine of this page, and the argument that connects them is a single claim: as generation gets cheap, the value of an additional option falls very fast, while the value of a sharper evaluation rises without limit. Everything that follows — the history, the mechanics, the arithmetic, the disagreements — is an elaboration of that claim and of where it breaks.

Section 2The idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

A working definition, stated tightly so it can be argued with. Taste is a standard for selection that a person can state before seeing the candidates, apply consistently across candidates, and defend to a competent peer who reaches a different conclusion. Editorial judgement is the exercise of that standard over a set of candidate artefacts, whose characteristic output is a reasoned rejection. Three things are excluded by that definition on purpose: private preference, which cannot be defended; authority, which does not need to be; and post-hoc rationalisation, which fails the "before seeing" clause.

The idea did not originate in technology. It is the professional core of editing, and editors formalised it long before software existed. Maxwell Perkins at Scribner's in the 1920s was valuable not for prose he wrote but for manuscripts he refused and cuts he insisted on. Film editing produced the most explicit version: Walter Murch's "rule of six", set out in In the Blink of an Eye (1995), ranks the criteria for choosing a cut — emotion, story, rhythm, eye-trace, two-dimensional plane, three-dimensional continuity — and assigns emotion 51 per cent of the weight, precisely because an editor facing several technically acceptable cuts needs a ranked principle rather than a feeling. Industrial design produced Dieter Rams's ten principles in the 1970s for the same reason: to turn "I prefer this" into an argument that a colleague could check. Software borrowed the vocabulary late and imprecisely, calling it "product sense" through the 2010s and mostly declining to define it, which is why the skill was hard to hire for and harder to teach.

What changed is a cost curve, not an insight. Through 2023–2026 the marginal cost of producing an adequate artefact — a screen, a paragraph of a specification, a query, a report voice, a cover image — fell by roughly two orders of magnitude, while the marginal cost of deciding which adequate artefact is right fell not at all. Kausalya's nine report voices took a day; the four weeks Devika then spent were entirely selection. That asymmetry is the whole of the "AI shift" as it bears on this topic.

Four schools disagree about what follows, and it is worth stating what each would and would not sign, because practitioners routinely argue past each other.

The connoisseurship school holds that taste is tacit knowledge acquired by prolonged exposure to excellent work under a master, and that reducing it to written criteria destroys the part that matters. It would sign: "any rubric complete enough to be useful is already too coarse to distinguish the best option from the second-best." It would not sign: "written standards are useless" — its adherents use exemplars heavily, just not criteria.

The decision-analytic school treats selection as a multi-attribute judgement problem contaminated by noise, and imports the machinery accordingly: decomposed criteria, independent scoring before discussion, aggregation last. Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony and Cass Sunstein's Noise (2021) is its most-cited statement in management, and its "mediating assessments protocol" is the direct ancestor of the scoring tables product teams now use. It would sign: "structured, decomposed, independent judgement is more reliable than holistic intuition, even when the intuition belongs to an expert." It would not sign: "the criteria list can ever be complete" — its honest members concede the residual.

The empiricist school holds that taste is a stopgap for the absence of data, and that any durable quality claim should be an experiment. It would sign: "a taste claim you cannot state as a testable prediction is not knowledge." It would not sign: "we should ship whatever wins the test irrespective of coherence" — though its critics attribute that to it, and some of its practitioners do behave that way.

The authorial school holds that the value of a product lies in the coherence of a single point of view, that coherence cannot be produced by aggregation, and that consistency across a thousand small decisions is what users perceive as quality. It would sign: "one named person must own the standard and be permitted to be wrong." It would not sign: "the market's average preference is the standard."

These four are not reconcilable by synthesis, and it is a mistake to pretend otherwise. They make different bets about where the residual — the part of quality no criterion captures — actually lives.

Section 3Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic

Expert practice, written out, is a pipeline of six operations, of which the third and fifth are usually invisible from outside. First, specify the moment: not "the service report" but "a facilities manager in Hyderabad forwarding this report, unedited, to a client's audit team at 9 p.m." Second, pre-register the standard: criteria and, crucially, disqualifiers, written before any candidate exists. Third, calibrate the raters — the step that is nearly always skipped. Fourth, generate along declared axes of variation. Fifth, eliminate on disqualifiers, then compare survivors pairwise on the ranked criterion. Sixth, record the kill notes and the sacrifice: which criterion the winner is knowingly weak on.

The formal treatment that makes sense of all six is straightforward, and once seen it is difficult to unsee. Model each candidate's true quality as a draw from a standard normal distribution — mean zero, standard deviation one — where "quality" means value against the standard you actually care about. Your evaluation of a candidate is not its true quality but a noisy reading of it: observed = true + error, where the error has standard deviation σ. You then pick the candidate with the highest observed value. Two quantities determine what you get.

The first is the expected maximum of n draws, which grows extremely slowly. For n = 5 it is about 1.16 standard deviations above the mean; n = 10 gives 1.54; n = 30 gives about 2.04; n = 100 gives 2.51. Going from ten options to a hundred — a tenfold increase in generation cost, and roughly a tenfold increase in review burden — buys you less than one standard deviation.

The second is the attenuation caused by evaluation noise. If you select on the observed value, the expected true quality of your pick is approximately the expected maximum divided by the square root of (1 + σ²). Call that factor ρ; it is the correlation between what you see and what is there. A team with a sharp, shared, pre-registered standard might achieve σ = 0.5, giving ρ = 0.89. A typical team arguing from taste in a two-hour review meeting is closer to σ = 1.0 (ρ = 0.71). A team with no shared standard, reviewing tired, at the end of a quarter, is plausibly at σ = 2.0 (ρ = 0.45). Table 1 multiplies the two.

Quality is modelled as a standard normal draw; evaluation adds independent normal error of standard deviation σ; selection is on the observed value. The attenuation factor ρ = 1/√(1+σ²). The model assumes candidates are independent, which generated options usually are not — see Section 6.

Read the table across, then down. A team at σ = 0.5 choosing among ten options lands at 1.38. A team at σ = 2.0 choosing among a thousand lands at 1.45 — barely better, having generated a hundred times as much and reviewed until nobody could see straight. The practical conclusion is uncomfortable for a profession that has spent three years celebrating throughput: halving your evaluation noise is worth more than multiplying your option count by a hundred. Devika's nine report voices were, on this reading, already plenty; her four weeks were correctly spent on sharpening the standard, not on generating a tenth.

The second-order effects are where it gets interesting. Reviewing more options raises σ, because attention degrades — so the two columns of Table 1 are not independent, and moving right along the rows tends to move you rightward across the noise columns too. Generated candidates are also correlated rather than independent: prompted from one brief by one model family, thirty candidates may contain six genuinely distinct approaches, in which case the effective n is six, not thirty. And there is a subtler effect that decision analysts call the optimiser's curse: when you select the maximum of noisy estimates, you systematically select candidates whose errors were favourable, so the winner's observed score overstates its true quality — and the more options you review, the worse the overstatement. Teams that celebrate "the data said variant 17 was 30 per cent better" over forty variants are usually celebrating noise.

Calibrating raters — the step nobody does — is what actually moves σ. The method is borrowed from content analysis and is cheap: give every reviewer the same eight candidates, including two the team already agrees are good and two it agrees are poor, have them score independently before any discussion, and decompose the variance. If the variance between raters on the same candidate exceeds the variance between candidates, there is no shared standard, whatever the wiki says. At Kausalya, Devika ran exactly this on the nine report voices: between-candidate variance was 0.61, between-rater variance was 0.94. Her conclusion was correct and unwelcome — the disagreement was not about the nine drafts, it was about what a service report is for, and no amount of further drafting would have surfaced it.

Section 4When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

Editorial judgement earns its keep under four conditions, each of which can be checked rather than assumed. Claim one: the differences between options are real but too small or too slow to measure. Applied to Kausalya, this holds decisively — 240 enterprise customers cannot be randomised, adoption shows up over quarters, and the report voice affects renewal conversations that happen once a year. Applied to Malhaar, it fails at the artefact level: a blurb's effect on play rate is measurable within hours across 62 lakh users. It holds at the level of the style, though, because Malhaar cannot test whether a house voice compounds into brand affection over three years.

Claim two: the option set is genuinely varied. Selection cannot improve on a set that contains one idea. Devika's nine voices differed on two declared axes and passed. Malhaar's generator, prompted from a single template, produced blurbs whose distinctness Sneha measured crudely and honestly: of a sample of 200, she could sort them into eleven recognisable patterns, so the effective variety was eleven.

Claim three: there exists a person or a written artefact that can adjudicate. Where no one is authorised to reject, the exercise degrades into consultation. Claim four: the cost of being wrong is recoverable. Where it is not — a hardware tooling freeze, a regulated disclosure, a contract term — the correct response is not sharper taste but more evidence and a slower decision.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. When the metric is honest, fast and high-powered, taste used instead of measurement is simply a slower, worse experiment. When the disagreement is really about strategy — which customer segment matters — dressing it as a taste argument hides the actual question and lets the loudest person win. And when the artefact is one of thousands generated per day, judging artefacts one at a time is not scaled-down editing; it is a category error, which is Rohit's whole problem.

Section 5Hard edge cases

Multi-product companies. Every product team optimises locally, and the locally best choice is usually the one that breaks the house voice. Mature companies handle this less elegantly than they claim: the published answer is a design system and a content style guide, and the actual answer is one or two named people who review anything customer-visible and whose calendar is the real constraint. The seam shows up as a queue.

Two-sided marketplaces. A single standard cannot serve two populations with opposed interests. The disciplined pattern is to score each candidate twice, from each side, and treat a large divergence as the finding rather than averaging it away. The failure pattern is a rubric written by the team that talks to the side with fewer, louder stakeholders — almost always supply.

Regulated products. In Indian financial services the disqualifier is often supplied from outside: mandated risk language for mutual-fund communication, disclosure requirements under insurance and securities regulation, the consent and notice obligations of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. This is a gift, not a constraint, because it forces at least one criterion to be written before generation. The edge case is subtler: teams start treating compliance as the entire standard, and ship copy that is defensible and unreadable.

Hardware plus software. Taste is committed at tooling freeze, twelve to eighteen months before a customer sees anything, and cannot be revised by a release train. Practitioners compensate by generating and rejecting far earlier and far more aggressively, and by holding the software layer as the adjustable part — which quietly loads the software team with every unresolved judgement from the hardware phase.

AI-native products. Here the artefact under judgement is not fixed. Malhaar's blurb generator does not have a voice; it has a distribution over voices. The correct object of editorial judgement is therefore the distribution's properties — its worst case, its variance, the frequency of specific failure classes — not any single sample. This is the deepest change the AI shift makes to the topic, and the least well handled in practice.

Figure 2. The ladder. Each step up multiplies leverage and lengthens the distance between the person with the standard and the artefact the customer sees.

Rohit's team climbed that ladder in eight weeks. Sneha's editors first judged blurbs, then wrote a standard of six rules, then built an automatic evaluator — a model prompted with the rules and with twenty labelled exemplars — which scored every generated blurb and suppressed the bottom decile. The critical discipline was the audit: Sneha continued to review a daily sample by hand, scoring blind, and tracked the agreement between her judgement and the evaluator's. In week one it was 62 per cent. By week six, after two rewrites of the rules, it was 84 per cent. The remaining 16 per cent was not noise; it was concentrated in the cases that mattered most, which is the pattern to expect.

The sampling arithmetic deserves stating, because teams get it wrong intuitively. If a specific failure class — say, a blurb that names a devotional artist alongside a party playlist during Ganesh Chaturthi — occurs in 2 per cent of outputs, and Sneha reviews a random 40 a day, the chance of catching at least one instance in a day is 1 − 0.98⁴⁰ = 55 per cent. To reach 95 per cent confidence of catching it, she needs 148 reviews. Random sampling is a poor instrument for rare, high-consequence failures; stratified sampling on risky segments is far better, and Malhaar eventually reviewed all festival-window and devotional-genre outputs while sampling the rest at 1 per cent.

Section 6Ten nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. Experts sharpen the evaluator; competent practitioners widen the funnel

The tell is the first request after a disappointing review. The competent practitioner asks for more options; the expert asks what the standard failed to capture. Table 1 explains why the expert is right, and the reason it feels wrong is that generating is visible work and calibrating is not.

2. Experts know that the residual is real and name it

Every rubric leaves something out — the part of quality that no criterion captured. The competent practitioner either denies the residual (and over-trusts the score) or hides behind it (and over-rules the score whenever convenient). The expert says explicitly: "the rubric ranks A above B; I am choosing B, and here is the unwritten criterion I am invoking." That sentence both preserves the discipline and updates it.

3. Experts treat polish as an artefact of production, not evidence of care

Before generation, finish correlated with effort, and effort correlated with thought. That inference is now void, and experts have visibly reset it: they read for the argument the artefact makes and are unmoved by clean type. The recognisable sign is a senior reviewer who asks "what is this choosing not to say?" before commenting on anything visual.

4. Experts distinguish disagreement about the standard from disagreement about the candidate

Most long review meetings are the first disguised as the second. The tell is that the argument keeps returning to an example nobody can settle. An expert stops the meeting and asks each person to write, in one line, what the artefact is for; the answers diverge, and the real meeting begins.

5. Experts hold consistency above cleverness

A team can plan around a chooser whose decisions it can predict, even an imperfect one. It cannot plan around a brilliant, unpredictable one, and it responds by producing safe work that will not be rejected. The measurable proxy — what fraction of your team can predict your pick before you make it — is worth tracking and is almost never tracked.

6. Experts distrust the winner's margin

Because of the optimiser's curse, the observed superiority of the selected option is inflated, and inflated more when more options were compared. Experts therefore discount the margin, plan for the shipped choice to underperform its review score, and are unsurprised when it does. The competent practitioner reports the review score to the leadership team as a forecast.

7. Experts write kill notes; competent practitioners write praise

Praise for the winner transmits almost nothing, because the winner's virtues are visible. The rejections carry the standard. An organisation that keeps its kill notes accumulates a training corpus for the next generation of PMs; one that keeps only its shipped work accumulates nothing.

8. Experts know that abundance can hide the absence of an idea

Thirty polished variants can be a substitute for one hard thought about the problem. The tell is that no variant is bad — genuine exploration produces some options that are clearly wrong, because they push an axis to its limit. A candidate set with no failures in it was not exploring; it was interpolating.

9. Experts pick the falsifying observation in advance

Not "we'll see how it does", but "if second-month retention does not move by 1.5 points and support contacts about the report do not fall, my standard was wrong, not just my pick." Very few practitioners separate those two failures, and the separation is the whole of learning.

10. Experts are explicit about what they sacrificed

A choice that gives up nothing has not been made. Devika's eventual decision, recorded in one paragraph, named the criterion she sacrificed — brevity — and predicted the complaint she would receive. When that complaint arrived from a large customer in April, it cost her nothing, because it was already on the record as a known price.

Section 7How the practice differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the loop is fast and the temptation is to let experiments carry everything. The real constraint is statistical power: at Malhaar's scale a 2 per cent difference in play rate is detectable in a day, but the differences that separate a good blurb from an excellent one are smaller than that, and a hundred simultaneous tests on small effects produce mostly false winners. Taste covers the region below the measurement floor, which is where most craft lives.

In enterprise B2B the loop is slow, the sample is small, and the buyer is not the user. Kausalya's standard has to include criteria a consumer PM never writes: whether an implementation partner can teach it in a two-hour session, whether it survives being pasted into a client's audit pack, whether a procurement reviewer in Dubai reads it as professional. Editorial judgement is doing more work here precisely because no experiment is available.

In platforms and marketplaces the difference is real and structural, as Section 5 described: two standards, and the divergence between them treated as information. In hardware the difference is one of timing and irreversibility rather than of kind. In AI-native products the difference is the deepest — the object of judgement is a distribution — and it is the one on which the profession has the least accumulated practice.

Stage matters more than most people expect, and the transition is sharp. Below roughly fifty people, the founder's taste is the standard, unwritten, and this is efficient. Between fifty and a few hundred, the founder becomes a queue and the organisation must externalise the standard or slow down; this is the transition most companies handle badly, usually by adding reviewers rather than writing criteria. Above that, the failure inverts: standards get written so abstractly that they disqualify nothing. If your published design principles cannot reject a real candidate that a team actually proposed last quarter, they are decoration.

Section 8Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Kausalya, the failure. In September 2025, before Devika joined, Kausalya shipped an earlier AI-drafted document: the annual maintenance summary sent to facility owners. The team had run a clean process — six candidates, a five-criterion rubric, weighted scores, a clear winner at 4.3 out of 5. Within three weeks, 38 of 240 customers had raised tickets. The chosen summary omitted the technician's certification identifier and the parts' serial numbers, because no criterion mentioned them; the rubric had been written by the product team, and the people who knew that these documents get folded into clients' own compliance packs sat in customer success in Singapore and had not been asked. The recovery took a full quarter: ₹42 lakh of engineering time, two escalations to the CEO, and one renewal delayed. What actually changed afterwards was not the rubric's weights but its structure — Kausalya moved from a purely weighted model to disqualifiers first, and made it a rule that the disqualifier list must be signed by whoever handles the artefact after the product team is done with it. The lesson is precise: weighted rubrics are good at ranking, and structurally incapable of noticing an absent criterion.

Kausalya, the recovery, in numbers. Applying the new structure to the nine report voices, four were eliminated on disqualifiers within twenty minutes — three omitted chain-of-custody fields, one placed the technician's free-text note where it would be truncated in a printed PDF. The five survivors were scored by seven raters, of whom three were outside product. Between-candidate variance rose to 0.88 and between-rater variance fell to 0.41 after a calibration round on two known-good and two known-poor exemplars. The winning voice led at 4.05 against 3.72 for the runner-up; Devika discounted both, expecting the true gap to be roughly half that, and it was.

Malhaar, at scale. Rohit's team measured what the editorial layer was worth rather than assuming it. In a two-week holdout across 4 lakh users, mixes with evaluator-filtered blurbs showed a play-through rate of 43.1 per cent against 41.4 per cent for unfiltered — 1.7 points, worth roughly ₹1.1 crore of annual retained subscription revenue on their arithmetic, against an editorial cost of about ₹68 lakh a year for five people. The number that persuaded the board, though, was different: complaints about tonally inappropriate blurbs during the Ganesh Chaturthi window fell from 214 to 19. Rare, high-consequence failures were where the human standard paid, and average quality was where it barely did.

The fourth row deserves emphasis because it is specific to the present moment. Once a team delegates first-pass selection to an automated evaluator, the standard stops being visible in anyone's behaviour. It drifts — the underlying model changes, the prompt is edited by someone tuning something else, the exemplar set ages — and nothing in the system announces the drift. The only instrument is a continuing human sample scored blind against the machine, with the agreement rate tracked as a first-class metric. Teams that build the evaluator and disband the editorial function have not automated taste; they have frozen a snapshot of last quarter's taste and stopped watching it.

Section 10Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether taste can be taught. The connoisseurship position, in its strongest form, is that judgement is acquired the way a language is: through immersion, correction and years, and that the written artefacts of a standard are at best scaffolding that the learner discards. Its evidence is the observable failure of rubric-trained reviewers to distinguish the best option from the second-best, and the fact that in every craft with a long history — editing, cooking, typography, architecture — the transmission mechanism is apprenticeship, not documentation. The opposing position, held by the decision-analytic school, is that most of the variance in real organisations is not between good and excellent but between shared and unshared standards, and that written criteria plus calibration reliably move the larger term. Its evidence is the noise literature and results like Devika's variance decomposition. What would have to be true for the connoisseurs to be wrong: that calibration on exemplars produces durable, transferable improvement in reviewers' rankings against a held-out expert panel. What would have to be true for the analysts to be wrong: that teams with tight rubrics converge on work that is reliably competent and reliably unremarkable — a claim for which the anecdotal evidence is strong and the systematic evidence thin.

Whether market feedback should override the standard. The empiricist steelman is that customers, not editors, determine value, and that a standard defended against measured preference is vanity. The authorial steelman is that measured preference is local and myopic — it reliably favours the familiar, and coherence compounds over horizons no experiment covers. Both are right in their own regimes, and the honest formulation of the disagreement is about the discount rate applied to coherence, which nobody can estimate.

Whether a model can hold a standard. One camp holds that an evaluator prompted with rules and exemplars is a legitimate carrier of taste, cheaper and more consistent than tired humans — and Malhaar's 84 per cent agreement is real evidence. The other holds that a model can only reproduce the distribution it was shown, so a model-as-judge locks in the past and cannot recognise the option that is good for reasons not yet articulated — which is precisely the case that matters. Note that both camps agree on the operational point, which is why the audit sample is not optional.

Section 11What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in ways an observer can see. They spend their preparation time before the options arrive, not after. They can state, in a sentence, what a given artefact is for, and their team can state the same sentence the same way. They reject quickly and explain briefly, and their rejections are predictable enough that people stop bringing work that will fail. They name the criterion they are sacrificing rather than pretending the choice was free. They are relaxed about being over-ruled on a candidate and immovable about being over-ruled on the standard without an argument. When a decision goes badly they are able to say which of the two things failed — the standard or the application of it — and they change the corresponding thing. And when volume rises, they climb the ladder in Figure 2 deliberately, keeping an audit sample the whole way, rather than discovering three quarters later that nobody has looked at what the machine is choosing.

Section 12What each protagonist decided

Devika chose the voice that leads with the fault code and the resolution in two lines, followed by the structured table — the least literary of the five survivors. Her reasoning: the artefact's real reader is not the technician's manager but a facilities auditor scanning forty reports, and for a scanning reader, structure beats prose. She recorded the sacrifice — the report reads coldly, and Kausalya's brand voice claims warmth — and the falsifying observation: if support contacts about report interpretation did not fall by at least a fifth by June, the standard, and not the pick, would be wrong.

Rohit chose neither to review everything nor to automate everything. Malhaar shipped the automated evaluator with a stratified human sample: 100 per cent review of festival windows, devotional and children's content, and 1 per cent elsewhere, with the agreement rate between Sneha's blind scores and the evaluator published weekly on the same dashboard as play-through rate. His stated reason was that the value of editorial judgement at scale sits in the tail, not the mean, and that an agreement rate is the only early warning available for a standard that has stopped being anyone's.

Three questions in the style of a teaching note.

1. Table 1 implies that Devika should have stopped generating at nine and spent everything on calibration. Under what conditions would that conclusion reverse — and could she have known she was in those conditions in advance?

2. Malhaar's evaluator agrees with Sneha 84 per cent of the time. Is that a good number? What would you need to know about the composition of the 16 per cent before answering, and what would make you shut the evaluator off?

3. Kausalya's failure was an absent criterion, which no weighting scheme can detect. Design a cheap organisational routine that would have caught it, and state what that routine would cost when it produces a false alarm.

Section 13Going deeper

Product sense and taste is the parent capability: this page treats selection under abundance, but the underlying question of what makes a product good sits upstream, and without it your criteria have no source. Reviewing work you did not write is the same skill applied line by line to text, specifications and code, and is where most PMs will spend their editorial hours; it unlocks the practical habits — reading for the argument, not the polish — that this page assumes. Reasoning about trade-offs gives you the vocabulary for the sacrifice clause: a choice that names what it gives up is a trade-off made explicit, and the discipline transfers directly.

What a junior PM should learn first now is the direct successor question: if selection has become the scarce skill and selection needs a standard, where does someone with no standard begin, and does the apprenticeship route still exist when nobody writes first drafts? Which PM skills repriced, up and down places this topic inside the broader shift and tells you which adjacent skills are worth your next quarter. Outsourcing your thinking to a model is the failure mode of this page taken to its conclusion — the practitioner who lets the generator set the standard as well as fill it — and it unlocks the self-diagnostics that keep the editor in the loop.

The prototype as the new specification and What a PRD becomes when the reader can build both concern artefacts that are now generated in quantity, and both require the standard-first discipline to be useful rather than voluminous. Velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved is the organisational counterpart to Figure 1 — it explains why teams shipping more feel slower. Chhaap Studio: two hundred good answers by Monday

Bengaluru, the night of Sunday 25 October 2026. A board meeting in fourteen hours, a Dubai contract in three weeks, and no agreement inside the company about what "good" means.

Section 1The night before

Aparna Deshpande had spread eleven printed sheets across the dining table in her flat in Indiranagar, which is not a thing she had done since business school. Diwali was a fortnight away and the lane outside was already testing its lights. On the sheets were forty-eight advertising creatives that Chhaap Studio's platform had produced that week for Chandrika Skinworks, a Coimbatore skincare brand with ₹64 crore of annual revenue and a listing on Nykaa that mattered more to it than its own website. Forty-eight of the two hundred and sixteen that Chhaap had generated for Chandrika's Diwali gifting campaign. Chandrika's brand manager had published four.

The board met at eleven the next morning. On the agenda was a single item that Rukmini Nair, Chhaap's co-founder and chief executive, had listed as Curate: go / no-go. Aparna, as chief product officer, owned the recommendation. She had written three versions of it during the day and deleted all three, because each one answered a question she was no longer sure was the right question.

The immediate facts were not in dispute. Chhaap generated more assets every quarter and its customers published a smaller fraction of them every quarter. Two large accounts had left in June. A Dubai contract worth ₹4.6 crore hung on a promise about brand consistency that Chhaap's product did not currently keep. And an internal study run by a twenty-six-year-old associate product manager had produced a finding that nobody in the leadership team had yet been willing to say out loud in a meeting.

Section 2Company history, and the decision that still binds

Chhaap Studio was founded in Bengaluru in 2020 by Rukmini Nair, who had run brand design at a large Indian consumer goods company, and Kabir Sheth, who had built imaging infrastructure at a photo-sharing app. The first product was unremarkable: templated packaging and catalogue photography for direct-to-consumer brands, executed by a small human studio in Jayanagar with software doing the tedious parts. It grew slowly and profitably to about ₹9 crore of revenue by early 2022.

The pivot came in the second half of 2022, when generative image and copy models became good enough that Chhaap could produce a plausible packaging concept, an ad creative or a landing-page hero without a designer touching it. Revenue tripled in four quarters. Two decisions taken in that period shape everything the company can do today.

The first was positioning. In March 2023 Rukmini wrote a page for the website that became, internally, scripture: Your brand, not ours. Chhaap would never impose a house style, never tell a brand what it should look like, and never put a designer's judgement between a brand manager and their own work. It was a genuine differentiator against the agencies, and it was also a promise that Chhaap's own taste would stay invisible. Sales built the pitch on it. Three of the company's ten largest customers say it is why they chose Chhaap.

The second was pricing. Chhaap charges per thousand generated assets, on a declining scale, with an annual minimum commitment. The model was chosen because it was legible to procurement teams and because it made expansion revenue automatic: a brand that ran more campaigns simply generated more. It also means that Chhaap's revenue is a function of how much the platform produces and not at all a function of how much of that production is any good. Every proposal to ship fewer, better assets is, mechanically, a proposal to bill less.

By September 2026 Chhaap served 412 brand customers, mostly Indian D2C companies in skincare, snacking, apparel and consumer electronics, with a growing set of mid-market accounts in the United States sold by a small team in New Jersey. Annual recurring revenue was ₹78 crore. Headcount was 190: engineering in Bengaluru and Pune, a nine-person design group led from Berlin, data science in Toronto, customer success in Singapore, sales in New Jersey and Mumbai.

Section 3The industry around it

Chhaap's customers live inside other people's storefronts. They sell on Nykaa, Amazon and Flipkart, they run performance campaigns on Meta and Google, they push quick-commerce listings onto Zepto and Blinkit where the creative is a single thumbnail seen for under a second, and the better-capitalised ones maintain their own sites on Shopify with payments through Razorpay. The volume of creative a mid-sized Indian D2C brand needs in a festive quarter has roughly quadrupled in four years, mostly because the number of surfaces has quadrupled.

Three forces bear directly on the decision. The first is that the cost of producing a creative asset has collapsed, which is why Chhaap exists, and which also means Chhaap's differentiation cannot be production. The second is regulatory: the Advertising Standards Council of India has been sharpening its guidance on substantiation of claims, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's consent and notice obligations have consumed six of Chhaap's engineers since May, because brands upload customer imagery and Chhaap must now prove provenance. Claim substantiation is a particular problem for generated copy, which will happily write "dermatologically tested" if the training distribution suggests skincare copy says that.

The third is competitive. Aakriti Creative Cloud, founded in Gurugram in 2024, sells the opposite proposition: one answer, not two hundred, with a human art director attached to every account. Aakriti is smaller — perhaps ₹22 crore in revenue — and more expensive per campaign. It took both of the accounts Chhaap lost in June.

Section 4The situation in detail

In January 2026 Chhaap shipped Infinite Variants, which raised the default output of a single creative brief from twenty assets to two hundred. The belief at the time, stated in the launch memo, was that brand managers were constrained by choice and would convert more of the option space into published work. Usage rose 3.4 times within a quarter. Revenue rose 61 per cent year on year. Exhibit 2 shows what else happened.

Section 5The people

Aparna Deshpande, chief product officer, Bengaluru, joined in 2024 from a large SaaS company. Her stated position is that Chhaap must "put judgement into the product". Her incentive is that Curate is her initiative and the board knows it. What she has not said is that she is no longer sure whether the thing she wants to encode is a standard or merely the design team's habits, and that Nikhil's Exhibit 4 has made this worse rather than better.

Rukmini Nair, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Her stated position is that "your brand, not ours" is the company's soul and that Chhaap must not become an agency. Her incentive is a Series C conversation in which the volume growth in Exhibit 2 is the headline. What she has not said is that the evaluator's rubric is substantially her own aesthetic, written down by Lena from two years of Rukmini's design reviews, and that she finds the ranked output persuasive in a way she has not examined.

Kabir Sheth, co-founder and VP engineering, Pune. His stated position is that the evaluator is ready and that shipping it as the default costs nothing. His incentive is that his platform team's roadmap for the next two quarters is built on it. What he has not said is that ranking is already silently active for about 6 per cent of traffic as a "latency experiment", which is where part of Exhibit 3's treatment group came from.

Lena Brandt, design director, Berlin. Her stated position is that selection is the craft and cannot be delegated to a model trained on median work; she wants a curated tier staffed by humans. Her incentive is that her nine-person team is the smallest function in the company and the only one whose headcount has not grown since 2024. What she has not said is that she has had two conversations with Aakriti Creative Cloud and has not decided anything.

Tanvi Krishnan, staff data scientist, Toronto. Her stated position is that the August result is directional and that a clean randomised test needs six weeks. Her incentive is professional: her name is on the deck whose summary slide overstated a result she had properly caveated. What she has not said is that she believes the true lift, adjusted for the selection into the beta, is closer to 5 per cent than 18, and that she has not been asked.

Wei-Ling Tan, head of customer success, Singapore. Her stated position is that customers want fewer and better and that the published-rate collapse in Exhibit 2 is a screaming signal. Her incentive is her renewal book, which carries ₹31 crore of the ₹78. What she has not said is that her two largest APAC accounts have already asked what discount they would get if their generation allowance fell, and that she does not have an answer.

Gaurav Malhotra, head of sales, New Jersey. His stated position is that volume is what wins mid-market RFPs in the United States and that a curated tier would give competitors a comparison Chhaap currently avoids. His incentive is the Al Qamra deal and his annual number. What he has not said is that in the August meeting in Dubai he described Chhaap's forthcoming "brand consistency guarantee" in terms that went beyond anything product had committed to.

Zoya Rahman, group brand head at Al Qamra Retail Group, Dubai, is not a Chhaap employee but is the most consequential voice in the room. Al Qamra runs department stores and a growing marketplace across the Gulf and wants Chhaap to produce creative for 180 house brands. Her stated requirement is that assets across those brands must be visibly consistent in quality even though they differ in style. She has asked, twice, who inside Chhaap is accountable for that consistency, and has not received a name.

Nikhil Rao, associate product manager, Bengaluru, ran Exhibit 4. His stated position is that the company does not have a written standard, only a rubric that was reverse-engineered from one person's preferences. His incentive is a promotion cycle in January. What he has not said is that when he ran the same sixty assets past three brand managers at customer accounts, their rankings correlated with the designers' at 0.22 — a number that appears in Exhibit 4 with no commentary attached.

Section 6Voices

"Honestly the two hundred are all fine. That's the issue. If ten were bad I could throw them out. Instead I sit there at eleven at night comparing bangle photographs and by the end I've stopped seeing anything at all." — Brand manager, Chandrika Skinworks, in a customer-success call, 14 September 2026
"0.44 vs 0.41. The model is already a better designer than our designers, on our own data. Can we please stop having this argument." — Kabir Sheth, #platform channel, 19 September 2026, 11:42 p.m. IST
